chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Barqi from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hisham ibn Salim who said:

I performed the Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, along with Ubaydullah ibn Rashid. I told him, 'Keep count for me.' So he began counting, going and returning, as one Shawt. When that reached us, I asked him, 'How do you count?' He said, 'Going and returning is one Shawt.' So we completed it as fourteen. Then we mentioned that to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he said, 'They have added to what is upon them, and there is no blame upon them.'

key_terms.أَبِي عَبْدِ اَللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah (Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, peace be upon him)
key_terms.زَادُوا: They added/exceeded (referring to the practice of counting)
key_terms.سَعَيْتُ: I performed Sa'i (ritual walking between Safa and Marwah)
key_terms.شَوْطاً: Shawt (a single circuit or leg of the Sa'i)
key_terms.لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِمْ شَيْءٌ: There is no blame/damnation upon them

ai.seo_question: How is one Shawt counted in the Sa'i ritual between Safa and Marwah?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* highlights the scholarly consensus on the definition of a 'Shawt' as a round trip, validating the common practice of counting fourteen circuits by treating each leg as half. Imam al-Sadiq’s response, 'They have added to what is upon them,' indicates that while the ritual is valid, the extra counting is a voluntary addition rather than an obligation, reflecting the Shia principle of ease in ritual worship. This clarifies the distinction between the minimum required acts and the customary practices adopted by the community.
